plot_extraction.response_text:
On a bitter winter night, the narrator visits his aspiring-author friend, Oberon, who has grown disgusted with his unpublished tales after repeated rejection by booksellers. Convinced that the stories have poisoned his happiness and contain something demonic, Oberon decides to destroy them. Despite briefly recalling the inspiration and imaginative pleasure behind his work, he drunkenly throws the manuscripts into the fire.

As the pages burn, Oberon sees his characters and visions in the flames, including the fiend he had created. He immediately regrets annihilating years of work and fears an aimless, forgotten life. Then the burning embers fly up the chimney and ignite the building’s roof, provoking a rapidly spreading fire alarm throughout the wind-lashed wooden town. Realizing that his manuscripts caused the blaze, Oberon’s despair turns to manic triumph: though no publisher would print his work, his imagination has literally set the town on fire.

style_extraction.response_text:
The story adopts a first-person, retrospective voice that is observant, urbane, and quietly ironic. The narrator participates in the action but functions chiefly as a foil and witness to Oberon’s emotional extravagance. His dry asides—often undercutting his friend’s lofty claims—create distance between what the characters profess and what the reader is invited to perceive. This produces a characteristic tonal mixture of sympathy and mockery: artistic despair is treated as psychologically real, yet also as theatrical, self-indulgent, and faintly absurd.

The prose is formal, literary, and distinctly nineteenth-century in cadence. Its diction combines elevated abstractions such as “retribution,” “conflagration,” and “incorporeal” with colloquial exclamations including “Pooh! Pish! Pshaw!” Sentences are often long and intricately balanced, using embedded clauses, cumulative lists, semicolons, dashes, and periodic constructions. These expansive sentences allow description, commentary, and comic qualification to coexist. In moments of excitement, however, the syntax contracts into fragments, repetitions, imperatives, and exclamations, accelerating the pace and dramatizing Oberon’s agitation.

Description is vivid, sensuous, and highly figurative. The opening winter scene is rendered through tactile cold, violent wind, frosted glass, hard pavements, and thundering wheels, while nautical metaphors turn the narrator’s wind-driven progress into a comic voyage. Fire becomes the dominant image and organizing symbol. It shifts from domestic comfort to purgation, spectacle, artistic vision, demonic agency, and finally public catastrophe. Cold and flame form a sustained contrast: the frozen town surrounds a heated interior in which imagination, alcohol, shame, and ambition intensify toward combustion.

The dialogue is stylized and rhetorically polished rather than strictly naturalistic. Oberon speaks in elaborate metaphors, literary allusions, apostrophes, and melodramatic self-condemnation, revealing a mind that instinctively converts experience into art even while renouncing authorship. The narrator replies with brevity, understatement, teasing literalism, and mock indignation. Their exchanges create much of the comedy, particularly through reversals: rejected manuscripts are imagined as demonic objects, bad writing as a spiritual curse, and commercial publishing as a field of villainy.

The narrative follows a carefully escalating comic-gothic structure. It begins in realistic social satire, moves into a chamber scene of confession and debate, intensifies through the ritual burning of the manuscripts, and culminates in an apparently supernatural consequence. Foreshadowing is embedded in the repeated language of devils, flames, enchantment, and possession. The final reversal transforms artistic failure into spectacular efficacy: the tales that could not attract a publisher literally set the town on fire. This ending depends on a pun made physical and gives Oberon the recognition he craves in grotesquely displaced form.

The dominant mode is comic Gothic, blended with literary satire and metafiction. Supernatural suggestion remains playfully ambiguous: the “fiend” may be an actual apparition, an imaginative projection, or simply the burning papers carried up the chimney. The story is self-conscious about composition, inspiration, revision, rejection, authorship, and the unstable value of literary work. It repeatedly dramatizes the gap between the ecstasy of creation and the disappointment of rereading, as well as the conflict between private imaginative conviction and public commercial judgment.

The characterization relies on contrast and caricatural amplification. Oberon is volatile, ambitious, self-lacerating, visionary, and addicted to grand gestures. His despair rapidly becomes rage, ecstasy, repentance, and triumph. The narrator is steadier and more skeptical, though he too is susceptible to imagination and spectacle. Secondary figures, especially the publishers, appear only through satirical summary and are reduced to comic types representing caution, philistinism, and commercial self-interest.

Allusion and analogy elevate and parody the situation simultaneously. References to Dante, Gray, Nebuchadnezzar, the Alexandrian manuscripts, witchcraft, fairy coin, and martyrdom lend cultural density while comically exaggerating the fate of an unpublished manuscript. Similes are frequent and expansive: ideas become buried jewels, inspiration becomes desert water, creative blockage becomes a wall of ice, and the manuscripts resemble a deformed infant. Such comparisons make inward mental states concrete and theatrical.

Overall, the style is ornate yet controlled, combining romantic imagery with skeptical humor. Its signature effect comes from allowing imaginative language to grow increasingly feverish while maintaining an ironic narrative frame. The result is a richly figurative, dialogue-driven satire in which artistic temperament is at once honored for its visionary power and exposed as vanity, obsession, and combustible excess.

generation.response_text:
The night on which Oberon burned his stories was one of those bitter nights when Winter, no longer content to pinch the noses of honest citizens and glaze the gutters for the destruction of elderly gentlemen, appears to have entered into a private compact with the winds for the general chastisement of mankind.

The snow had ceased at dusk; but the cold increased after it, tightening the town as a screw tightens a coffin-lid. The pavements rang beneath the foot. Every pane was blind with frost, every pump wore an icy beard, and the moon, sailing among torn black clouds, looked as hard and polished as a silver coin which no charitable hand had ever warmed. The wind came roaring down the narrow streets, caught me by the skirts, turned me half about, and then, discovering that I persisted in my course, drove me toward Oberon’s lodging with such violence that I may be said to have arrived under sail.

I crossed the market-place like a small vessel making dangerous water. Carts thundered past me; signs creaked overhead; chimney-pots groaned; and once a slate, detached from some invisible roof, struck the stones at my heel and flew into fragments. I took this for an omen, though of what I could not then determine. A man commonly interprets an omen after the event; before it, he is merely annoyed.

Oberon inhabited the upper floor of a wooden house in Griffin Street, over a maker of coffins and opposite a dealer in lamps—a position which, as I often told him, placed him conveniently between death and illumination. He never thanked me for the observation. On this evening I found the outer door unfastened, climbed the crooked stair, and knocked twice.

“Enter,” cried a voice of sepulchral magnificence.

I entered and saw my friend seated before an enormous fire.

The room was poor, but ambitious. Books in uncertain battalions occupied the chairs, the table, the window-sill, and much of the floor. A plaster bust of Shakespeare, cracked across the forehead, presided over the mantelpiece; beneath him stood an empty bottle, two full bottles, a chipped glass, and a brass candlestick whose flame was beaten sideways whenever the wind found entrance through the casement. The fire alone was magnificent. It leaped and bellowed in the chimney, making the mean walls alternately golden and black.

Oberon sat in a faded dressing-gown, his hair disordered, his cheek flushed, and his eyes fixed upon a heap of manuscripts tied with blue, red, and yellow ribbons. I knew those packets. I had seen some of them born, watched others languish through infancy, and had even carried one—an unfortunate romance in three volumes—to a bookseller who returned it with such speed that I suspected he had hurled it from an upper window.

“You are late,” said Oberon.

“The wind opposed me.”

“The wind!” he exclaimed. “The wind is a critic, then. It seeks to drive every man backward.”

“Not every man. I saw it greatly assist a hat.”

He frowned, but pushed a glass toward me. I took it, for the room, despite the fire, retained in its corners several colonies of cold.

“You find me,” he said, “at the close.”

“The close of the bottle?”

“The close of a career.”

“Ah. Which career?”

He waved his hand toward the manuscripts. “That fever, that folly, that splendid degradation which I have called authorship.”

As no printer had yet called it authorship, I judged his definition liberal; nevertheless, there are hours when contradiction is cruelty, and others when it is merely useless. This was both.

He rose and began to pace the room, stepping over books with the instinctive accuracy of a cat among flower-pots.

“Look at them,” he said. “There lie eight years of servitude. Eight years! While other men ate, I imagined banquets; while they loved, I constructed heroines; while they slept, I argued with phantoms. I have poured my youth into those pages as the alchemist poured his estate into the furnace—and with the same result: smoke, ashes, and creditors.”

“Not wholly the same. The alchemist occasionally exploded.”

“Pooh! Pish! Pshaw! You jest beside an open grave.”

I glanced at the coffin-maker’s sign visible through the frozen pane. “An upper grave, perhaps.”

He stopped before me.

“You do not understand. No one understands. The booksellers least of all. I have taken these tales from counter to counter, from sanctum to sanctum, from one upholstered tribunal of ignorance to another. One says the public dislikes sorrow; another, that the public will tolerate nothing else. One demands action; another complains that my action fatigues him. A third praises my imagination with the air of a physician admiring the complexion of a dying man, and regrets that imagination cannot be made commercially useful.”

“Did none offer to publish?”

“One offered—on condition that I should pay for paper, printing, advertisements, binding, storage, carriage, and the probable demolition of his reputation.”

“A cautious patron.”

“A villain! A cold-blooded trafficker in immortality! He weighs genius by the pound, rejects Homer for bulk, Dante for gloom, and Shakespeare because the plays are already known.”

Here Oberon drained his glass, replenished it, and held it up against the fire as though examining some ruby medicine for despair.

“They have poisoned me,” he continued more quietly.

“The booksellers?”

“The tales.”

This answer, being less reasonable than the former, alarmed me more.

“They have poisoned my happiness,” he said. “They creep after me. Their unwritten endings whisper beneath my pillow; their discarded scenes grin from the walls; their phrases return at dinner and make the meat taste of ink. There is something demonic in them—yes, demonic! I conceived them, but they have possessed me. I am no longer their author. I am their habitation.”

“You are also their landlord. Evict them.”

“I shall.”

He pointed to the fire.

Until that moment I had regarded his despair as one regards a thunderstorm heard at a safe distance: impressive, musical, and unlikely to wet one’s coat. But now I looked from the manuscripts to the grate and perceived that his rhetoric had acquired an intention.

“You cannot mean to burn them.”

“I can. I do. I must.”

“Why?”

“Because they are false idols.”

“Then sell them as antiquities.”

“Because they are deformed offspring.”

“That is no reason to roast them.”

“Because they are fiends!”

“Fiends tied with blue ribbon?”

“The devil has worn finer decorations.”

He seized the uppermost packet, but did not immediately cast it in. His fingers lingered on the knot. On the wrapper was written, in a large hand, *The Kingdom Under Glass: A Romance*. I remembered the summer in which he had composed it. We had then lodged near a lake whose surface, at dawn, lay so still that mountains seemed to descend beneath it into another sky. Oberon, looking into that incorporeal country, had declared that a drowned kingdom existed below, inhabited by pale kings, bells without sound, and women who remembered the future. For six weeks he had been happy.

“This one came to you by the lake,” I said.

He stared at the title.

“Yes,” he murmured. “The morning was blue. Do you remember the reeds? They shivered though there was no wind. I saw the palace distinctly—every tower inverted, every window blazing downward into the deep.”

“And you wrote ten chapters before breakfast.”

“Twelve.”

“Eleven and a preface.”

A reluctant smile troubled his mouth. For a moment the room softened. He untied the ribbon and turned the pages. Here were his corrections, his vehement marginal commandments, his arrows, insertions, excommunications, and repentances. A manuscript after revision resembles a battlefield upon which grammar has defeated the author at considerable cost to both.

He read a passage under his breath. The old light entered his eyes.

“There was beauty in the conception,” he said.

“Much beauty.”

“The queen who could speak only in reflections—”

“Excellent.”

“And the bronze divers descending by moonlight—”

“Unforgettable.”

“You said they delayed the plot.”

“They delayed it beautifully.”

His smile vanished. “Yet they refused it.”

“Booksellers are not bronze divers.”

“They called it obscure.”

“They fear water.”

He flung the packet upon the table.

“No! You tempt me backward. That pleasure was the bait; this misery is the hook. Inspiration! What is it? A cup of water discovered in a desert, delicious because one is perishing, and gone before one knows whether it was water or a mirage. Composition is enchantment; revision, awakening; publication—ha! publication is the locked gate before which the naked dreamer discovers a notice forbidding trespass.”

He snatched another bundle.

“Here is *The Bell of Saint Orison*. I heard that bell in sleep for three years. Here is *The Widow’s Lantern*, written while my mother lay dying. Here, *The Last Masque of Nebuchadnezzar*—rejected as improbable by a man who publishes parliamentary speeches! Here are my martyrs, my witches, my gray abbots, my children born old, my dead who would not remain decorously buried. Shall they pursue me forever?”

“They have remained very quiet on the table.”

“That is their cunning.”

He drank again. The fire struck upward, impatient as a creditor.

I attempted persuasion. I spoke of time, revision, changing taste, future recognition, and the many admirable works which had endured neglect before triumphing over posterity. These arguments, being ancient, respectable, and of no practical use whatever, affected him as rain affects a statue.

“Posterity!” he cried. “The graveyard of unpaid accounts! Must I dine on future praise? Shall I warm myself at unborn admiration? Will a bookseller in the year two thousand send me royalties backward through eternity?”

“Postal arrangements may improve.”

“Mock me! It is fitting. I am already a comic figure—the lean poet at the fat merchant’s door, the conjurer whose fairy coin turns to leaves at noon. But I shall be free. Tonight I perform my own deliverance. Let Alexandria burn again, though its library occupy one table and contain no work approved by reviewers!”

Before I could prevent him, he thrust *The Kingdom Under Glass* into the grate.

The ribbon caught first, curling into a small blue serpent. Then flame seized the wrapper, raced along the edges, and opened the packet leaf by leaf. The close-written pages blackened; sentences glowed crimson for an instant, each word legible in fire, then broke into scales of ash. Oberon leaned over them with a countenance compounded of priest, murderer, and cook.

“There,” he said hoarsely. “The kingdom has fallen.”

“It appears to burn upward.”

“The laws of nature insult me even now.”

He added *The Bell of Saint Orison*. The fire rang no bell, but gave a hollow report as air escaped between the sheets. Then followed *The Widow’s Lantern*, which produced, by an accident of ink or gum, a green flame. At this Oberon recoiled.

“Did you see?”

“Copper in the coloring, perhaps.”

“It was her lantern!”

“It was chemistry.”

“Chemistry is the superstition of materialists.”

Packet after packet went in. I rescued one from his hand and asked whether he had no copy.

“None.”

“No draft?”

“Burned last spring.”

“No notes?”

“Torn.”

“Then at least allow me to preserve this.”

He read the title: *The Fiend of Ashenbridge*.

His face altered.

“That least of all.”

“Why?”

“Because it contains him.”

“Him?”

“The thing I made and could not unmake.”

I had read part of that tale. Its villain was a shadowy being who entered houses through chimneys, feeding upon unwritten thoughts and leaving sparks in men’s brains. I had considered him picturesque, though too fond of speeches.

“Oberon,” I said, “your fiend is ink.”

“Ink is merely darkness made fluid.”

“And paper?”

“The grave-cloth of ideas.”

“Your definitions grow dangerous.”

He tore the packet from me.

“The bookseller laughed at him. Laughed! He said my monster could not frighten a child of seven. Let him go, then. Let him return to his element.”

He hurled the tale into the heart of the blaze.

For several moments neither of us spoke. The papers swelled, collapsed, and sent forth a multitude of little flaming fragments. The room filled with the bitter odor of scorched ink and sealing-wax. Outside, the wind struck the house broadside, making the rafters complain.

Oberon watched with terrible attention.

“There!” he whispered.

“What?”

“The bridge.”

I saw only two charred sheets leaning together.

“And beneath it—the river! The horsemen! Look, look! The black tower is opening.”

The burning leaves, lifted and folded by heat, did indeed assume fleeting architectures. A turret sprang up and perished; a face glimmered in profile; a procession of red figures ran along a margin and plunged into darkness. The imagination which had created the tales now fought to preserve them, transforming their destruction into one final, magnificent edition.

Oberon extended both hands.

“My people,” he cried. “They are coming out! The queen beneath the lake—her glass crown melts! The widow lifts her lamp. Old Father Anselm walks through the coals. Ah, my little prince, I had forgotten you!”

I confess that I, too, saw something—not what he named, perhaps, but enough to understand him. Flame is the oldest romancer. Give it a rag, a twig, a crumpled page, and it builds cities more splendid than ours, peoples them, conquers them, and destroys them before the sober eye can object.

Then a black shape rose in the grate.

It gathered itself from the burning manuscript, a crooked body with long arms and a pointed head; two holes shone where eyes might have been. It leaned toward us, wavering, enlarged, and for one absurd yet unpleasant instant seemed to grin.

“The fiend!” shouted Oberon.

A gust descended the chimney. The shape burst apart. Half flew into the room as ash; half shot upward in a whirl of sparks.

Oberon staggered back and struck the table. The bottle fell, but I caught it—a service to literature for which I have never received acknowledgment.

“It is done,” he said.

The rage had left him. His face, a moment before illuminated by sacrifice, now appeared exhausted and old. He sank into the chair and stared at the grate, where red embers consumed the last corners of his labor.

“What have I done?”

“What you repeatedly announced you would do.”

“Eight years.”

“Yes.”

“Gone.”

“Very nearly.”

He dropped to his knees and thrust the tongs among the coals. He dragged out a smoking fragment, slapped it with his hand, read three surviving words, and uttered a sound more piteous than any in his fiction.

“‘And she remembered—’ Remembered what? I shall never know!”

“You wrote it.”

“But I have forgotten!”

He searched frantically through the ash. Black leaves broke at his touch. A sentence, glowing along one edge, vanished while he read it. He caught at scraps as a miser might catch banknotes in a gale.

“My kingdom! My bells! My dead! Fool—assassin—barbarian! Worse than the caliph who burned Alexandria, for he may at least have disliked reading. I have murdered the only witnesses that I ever lived.”

“You remain alive.”

“For what? To eat, sleep, grow bald, and be forgotten by persons who never heard of me? A man’s life is a corridor between two locked doors unless he hangs some picture on the wall. Mine were poor pictures, perhaps—but they were mine!”

A distant cry arose in the street.

Oberon did not hear it. He sat amid the ashes, mourning with an extravagance which would have been ludicrous had it not been sincere—and which, being sincere, was only partly ludicrous.

The cry came again, nearer and multiplied.

“Fire!”

I went to the window. Against the frosted glass a reddish pulse appeared and vanished.

“Fire!” shouted voices below. “Wake! Fire!”

A bell began to clang. Another answered from beyond the market-place; then another, until the whole frozen town seemed filled with iron tongues. Doors burst open. Men ran half-dressed into the street. Women called from upper windows. The wind, delighted to exchange cold mischief for hot, roared among the roofs.

I opened the casement. Smoke descended upon us.

“The roof,” I said.

“What?”

“Our roof is burning.”

We ran to the landing. Already feet thundered on the stairs. The coffin-maker appeared in his nightshirt, carrying a mallet in one hand and a child in the other. Behind him came his wife with a clock, then his apprentice with nothing but his boots.

“Out!” he shouted. “The sparks have fired the shingles!”

Oberon stood motionless.

“Sparks?” he repeated.

“From your chimney, curse you! The roof’s ablaze!”

A burning fragment sailed past the stair window like a crimson moth and lodged beneath the eaves of the neighboring warehouse. Almost instantly a thread of flame ran along the dry wood. The wind seized it, flattened it, stretched it, and flung it onward.

We descended into Griffin Street. Above us Oberon’s roof was a red, ragged crown. Fire streamed from it horizontally, as banners stream in battle. The lamp-dealer’s sign ignited; his stock, faithful to its profession, contributed an astonishing brightness. Across the lane, sparks settled upon a stable. Horses screamed. Men formed lines at the pumps, but the water froze upon the stones or flew backward in the gale. Shingles leaped from roof to roof. Windows reddened, cracked, and burst.

“Your manuscripts,” I said. “The burning leaves went up the chimney.”

Oberon looked at me, then at the town.

The conflagration had already crossed the market-place. Bells clamored; engines rattled; wheels thundered over the iron pavement. Citizens rushed about with blankets, buckets, ladders, portraits of ancestors, cages of birds, ledgers, cradles, and objects chosen in that sublime confusion which reveals what each soul considers indispensable. One banker saved a stuffed owl and abandoned his account books. A philosopher carried three volumes of metaphysics into the street, returned for the fourth, and found the staircase gone.

The fire mounted higher. It shone upon the snow, turning winter into a ghastly summer. Chimneys stood black against the blaze like monuments erected before the battle had ended.

Oberon’s despair slowly changed.

His shoulders straightened. His eyes widened. The flames of Griffin Street entered them and found congenial lodging. He began to laugh—not loudly at first, but with a low, amazed delight.

“What is it?” I demanded.

“They refused them.”

“This is hardly the moment—”

“They said my tales had no power.”

“Oberon—”

“They said they would kindle no interest!”

A roof fell with a roar, sending a tower of sparks into the heavens.

He sprang upon a water-butt and lifted both arms toward the blazing town.

“Behold!” he cried. “No publisher would print me, no critic praise me, no public buy me—but I have my readers now! Roof, window, steeple, street—every one illuminated! They called my imagination cold. Cold! Ha! It has set the town on fire!”

Then, while buckets passed beneath him and respectable citizens shouted for him to come down and make himself useful, Oberon stood exultant amid the snow and sparks, crowned by that dreadful light—an author at last successful, though in an edition which no bookseller could return.

free_generation.response_text:
The Town That Borrowed Tomorrow

On the first Tuesday of every month, the future arrived in Bellwether by train.

It came at six in the morning, when fog lay thick over the river and the station lamps still burned. The engine was always black, though no soot marked its chimney, and it made no sound except for a soft ticking, like a watch wrapped in cloth.

No passengers ever stepped onto the platform. Only parcels.

There were usually a dozen: brown boxes tied with white string, each labeled with the name of someone in town. The stationmaster placed them on a brass cart and rang the bell.

By breakfast, everyone knew who had received something from tomorrow.

A farmer might find a jar of next season’s honey and learn whether the clover would bloom. A widow might receive a newspaper and see her own name absent from the death notices. Children sometimes opened boxes containing schoolbooks with answers written in their older handwriting. Once, Mayor Vale received a photograph of the town square with a marble statue of himself in the center. He ordered the pedestal built that afternoon.

There were rules.

A parcel could come only from one day ahead. Nothing living could be sent. No weapons were permitted, though no one knew who enforced this. And every object borrowed from tomorrow had to be returned before midnight.

At eleven fifty-five each night, the recipients gathered at the station. The black train arrived from the opposite direction, silent as before, and the borrowed things were placed back inside. If a parcel was not returned, tomorrow would not come.

This last rule was painted in red above the station doors.

RETURN WHAT IS NOT YET YOURS.

No one knew what would happen if they failed. No one wished to find out.

For thirty-seven years, Bellwether borrowed tomorrow without incident.

Then Mara Venn received a letter from her dead mother.

Mara was the town clockmaker. She lived above her shop on Pendulum Street, among the patient breathing of clocks. Her mother, Elian, had died twelve years earlier, after a winter illness that no medicine could cure. Mara had been nineteen then, old enough to understand death and young enough to believe understanding made it easier.

It had not.

On the first Tuesday of October, the stationmaster delivered a narrow parcel to Mara’s shop. It was light and flat, and her name was written across the paper in a hand she recognized before she admitted recognizing it.

Mara Venn.

The final n curled downward. Her mother had always done that.

Mara locked the shop door.

For several minutes she stood behind the counter, listening to a hundred clocks disagree about the hour. Then she cut the white string.

Inside the parcel was an envelope.

My dearest Mara, it said on the front.

Her knees weakened. She sat on the floor.

The letter within was four pages long.

Her mother wrote of ordinary things. The pears in the eastern orchard had ripened early. The kitchen roof still leaked above the stove. She had misplaced her blue scarf and suspected Mara’s father had used it to polish his boots. She asked whether Mara still bit the inside of her cheek while repairing difficult mechanisms.

Then the letter became stranger.

I do not know how this reaches you, Elian wrote. For me, it is Monday evening, and you are asleep upstairs. You are nineteen. The doctor says I may have another week. Perhaps two. A man came to the door at dusk. He wore a conductor’s uniform and told me I could send one thing forward, but only if someone sent it back. I asked how far. He said, “As far as grief requires.”

Mara stopped reading.

Outside, someone tried the shop door. A customer called her name and went away.

She looked again at the handwriting.

You will want to keep this letter. You must not.

The words blurred.

Return it tonight. If you do, another letter will come next month. I have been promised twelve. If you keep any one of them, it will be the last.

Mara read the letter twice more. By noon, she knew every line. By evening, she could hear her mother’s voice in every turn of phrase.

At eleven fifty, she walked to the station with the envelope hidden inside her coat.

The platform was crowded. Mayor Vale had borrowed tomorrow’s election results and looked pleased. A baker carried a loaf made from dough that had not yet risen. Two brothers argued over a racing form. Near the luggage cart, a little girl clutched a glass globe containing snow that would not fall until the following day.

The stationmaster, Mr. Rook, checked each object against his ledger.

“Letter,” he said when Mara approached.

She held it tighter. “Where did it come from?”

“Tomorrow.”

“No. When did it come from?”

Mr. Rook studied her over his spectacles. He was an old man with a long, narrow face and silver hair combed neatly behind his ears.

“You know I cannot answer questions about the line.”

“My mother wrote it twelve years ago.”

“Then perhaps twelve years ago is tomorrow somewhere.”

“That makes no sense.”

“Railways rarely do when viewed from the platform.”

The train appeared through the fog. Its single lamp shone pale and round. The ticking grew louder.

Mara looked down at the envelope.

“I could keep it,” she whispered.

Mr. Rook closed his ledger. “You could.”

“What would happen?”

“I don’t know.”

“Has no one ever tried?”

“Not in Bellwether.”

The train stopped.

Its doors opened onto darkness.

Mara thought of the years since her mother’s death: birthdays without her, winters without her, the clock shop inherited too soon. She thought of all the questions she had saved for a person who could no longer answer. Twelve letters. Twelve months in which her mother might become, for a few hours at a time, more than memory.

She placed the envelope on the cart.

Mr. Rook rolled it into the dark.

The doors shut. The train departed.

At midnight, every clock in Bellwether struck twelve.

Tomorrow came.

The second letter arrived in November.

Elian wrote about Mara’s childhood: the time she had dismantled the hall clock at age six and hidden the springs under her pillow; the summer she tried to teach a goat to dance; the night she asked whether stars were holes through which the dead watched the living.

I told you no, the letter said. I did not want you to think heaven was spying. But lately I wonder if love is a kind of watching. Not judgment. Attention.

The third letter came in December. The fourth in January.

Mara returned each one.

She began living from Tuesday to Tuesday, from parcel to parcel. Customers noticed that she smiled more often. She repaired clocks ahead of schedule. She bought pears even when they were out of season.

In February, her mother wrote about fear.

I am afraid of dying, though everyone praises courage as if fear were a failure of character. I think courage may simply be fear that has put on its boots.

In March, she wrote about Mara’s father, who had left when Mara was nine.

In April, she apologized for being impatient.

In May, she described a dream in which they met as old women beside a green sea.

Then came June.

The train arrived on time. Mr. Rook unloaded eleven parcels and frowned.

Mara waited beside the brass cart.

“That’s all,” he said.

“There should be one for me.”

“There is no other cargo.”

“You missed it.”

“I did not.”

She stepped toward the train, but the doors had already closed. The black engine slipped away into the morning.

All day, Mara moved through the town as though walking underwater. She checked the station three times. She searched the post office, questioned the conductor of the noon train, and opened her empty mailbox until dusk.

That night, she confronted Mr. Rook.

“You said there would be twelve.”

“I said no such thing.”

“She did.”

He removed his spectacles and polished them. “Perhaps the letter was lost.”

“On a train from tomorrow?”

“Tomorrow loses many things.”

“Can I send something back?”

“No.”

“Why not?”

“The line carries loans, not messages.”

“The letters are messages.”

“The letters are cargo.”

Mara struck the counter with her palm. “That is a distinction made by a coward.”

Mr. Rook’s expression did not change, but his hand stopped polishing the glass.

“Yes,” he said. “Most rules are.”

Mara left before she said something worse.

The seventh letter arrived in July.

There was no explanation for the missed month. Her mother wrote as though the sequence were unbroken. She described rain against the windows, the taste of mint tea, and the sound of nineteen-year-old Mara sleeping in the next room.

Mara read the pages carefully. Near the end, one sentence had been underlined.

The conductor says the track is weakening.

At eleven fifty-five, Mara stood alone at the far end of the platform.

She watched townspeople return their borrowed objects. Mayor Vale surrendered a speech applauded by an audience that did not yet exist. A young couple returned a key to a house they hoped to buy. The baker carried an empty cake box, having eaten the contents despite the rule that objects should remain unchanged. Mr. Rook merely sighed and marked his ledger.

Mara took out the letter.

The train arrived.

She imagined walking away. She imagined hiding the pages under a floorboard or locking them inside a clock. What could the train do? Stop tomorrow? The idea seemed childish, a threat told to keep an obedient town obedient.

Yet the letter itself was impossible. Her mother’s handwriting was impossible. The black train, the future newspapers, the snow globe filled with Wednesday’s storm—all impossible.

One impossibility could enforce another.

She returned the letter.

August brought the eighth.

The track is weakening because too much has been borrowed, Elian wrote. Not objects. Certainty.

She explained that the conductor had visited again. Bellwether had spent decades looking ahead, choosing only roads that promised success. Farmers planted crops after seeing the harvest. Merchants stocked what tomorrow’s customers demanded. Lovers proposed only after glimpsing acceptance. Elections were decided before votes were cast. Risks vanished. So did accidents, surprises, and acts of faith.

A town cannot live forever on confirmed decisions, Elian wrote. Tomorrow must be allowed to arrive unopened.

Mara read the sentence aloud.

That afternoon, she walked through Bellwether.

She saw things she had always seen without noticing. The florist displayed bouquets copied from photographs of tomorrow’s weddings. Boys outside the betting shop traded information from future scores. At the council hall, Mayor Vale reviewed a transcript of the next day’s debate and rehearsed his cleverest replies.

No one wondered anymore.

No one guessed.

At the schoolyard, children played a game called Prediction. One child named an action; the others consulted slips of paper borrowed from the next day and declared whether it would succeed. When a boy proposed climbing the old cedar tree, a girl checked her paper.

“You fall,” she said.

The boy stepped away from the trunk.

“Does it say I’m hurt?”

“No.”

“Then maybe I should climb.”

“But you fall.”

He did not climb.

In September, the ninth letter contained only two paragraphs.

The conductor says one letter will not reach you. I do not know which. He says a missing thing is sometimes more important than an arriving one.

Then:

Mara, when the last letter comes, you will be asked to choose. Do not choose for me.

The rest of the pages were blank.

Mara took the letter to Mr. Rook.

“What choice?”

He looked older than he had the month before. Deep shadows hung beneath his eyes.

“I cannot tell you.”

“Cannot or will not?”

“Both.”

“Is the train dangerous?”

“Yes.”

“To me?”

“To everything.”

She leaned across the counter. “Then why have you spent thirty-seven years unloading it?”

“Because the first parcel had my name on it.”

He opened a drawer and removed a child’s red mitten. The wool was faded, and one thumb had been clumsily mended.

“My daughter disappeared when she was seven,” he said. “We searched the river, the forest, every road. Then the train came. It brought this from the following day.”

Mara touched the mitten.

“You found her?”

“No. But each month, another object arrived. A ribbon. A shoe. Once, a drawing of a house under three suns. I thought the next parcel would tell me where she had gone.”

“Did it?”

“After a year, they stopped. By then the town had seen what the train could do. People demanded that I keep the route open.”

“And your daughter?”

Mr. Rook looked toward the tracks.

“She would be forty-four now. Some mornings, I think she is the conductor.”

October arrived cold and clear.

The tenth letter warned that the final train would come in December.

November’s letter was the longest. Elian wrote of everything she wished she could have lived to see: Mara’s first gray hair, the changing town, inventions not yet imagined, the person her daughter would become without a mother to witness it.

But perhaps that is what children are, she wrote. Futures their parents cannot visit.

Mara wept until the ink ran beneath her fingers.

Before returning the letter, she added three words at the bottom.

I miss you.

She knew the rules. She knew borrowed objects had to be returned unchanged. Still, she folded the pages and placed them on the cart.

Mr. Rook saw the addition. He said nothing.

The train carried the message into darkness.

On the first Tuesday of December, every person in Bellwether gathered at the station.

No parcels had arrived for anyone except Mara.

Her box was small.

Inside lay the twelfth letter and a brass lever no longer than her hand.

The letter began:

My dearest Mara,

Your words appeared on the page.

I miss you.

For me, you wrote them before I died. For you, I imagine many years have passed. I cannot explain what it means to hear from the woman my daughter became. I can only tell you that, for one moment, death feels less like a wall than a door we are standing on opposite sides of.

The conductor has offered us a bargain.

Keep the lever, and the line will remain open. More letters may come—not only from me, but from anyone who has been lost. Bellwether will continue to receive tomorrow.

Return the lever, and the train will never stop here again.

You may think you are choosing whether to lose me. You are not. You lost me twelve years ago.

You are choosing whether to let tomorrow belong to the living.

The station was silent when Mara finished reading.

Everyone had heard of the lever by then. Rumors moved quickly in Bellwether, especially rumors about the future.

Mayor Vale pushed through the crowd.

“You cannot return it,” he said.

A murmur of agreement followed.

“My office relies on those reports.”

“So does my farm,” called someone else.

“My husband is ill,” said a woman near the door. “Tomorrow’s tests tell us whether the medicine works.”

A shopkeeper raised his voice. “The train belongs to the town.”

“It came to me,” Mara said.

“But the choice affects us all.”

“Yes.”

“Then we vote,” Mayor Vale declared.

Mr. Rook stood behind his counter, ledger closed.

“No,” he said.

The mayor stared at him. “No?”

“The railway does not recognize elections.”

The platform clock showed eleven forty-eight.

People surrounded Mara. They pleaded, argued, threatened. A man offered her his house. The baker promised free bread for life. The sick woman took Mara’s hand and asked whether uncertainty was worth dying for.

Mara had no answer.

At eleven fifty-three, the ticking began beyond the fog.

She looked at the lever.

With it, she might hear from her mother again. There could be thirteen letters. A hundred. Perhaps one day the train would bring a photograph, a voice recorded on some future device, a way to cross the door entirely.

But she remembered the boy beneath the cedar tree.

You fall.

He had accepted those words as a command.

The train emerged.

Mayor Vale seized Mara’s wrist.

“For once,” he said, “think about tomorrow.”

Mara looked at him.

“We have done nothing else for thirty-seven years.”

She pulled free.

The train stopped, and its doors opened.

For the first time, a conductor stood inside.

The figure wore a dark uniform with silver buttons. Beneath the cap was the face of a woman neither young nor old. Mr. Rook made a broken sound.

The conductor looked at him but did not speak.

Mara stepped forward.

In one hand she held the lever. In the other, her mother’s final letter.

She wanted to keep both.

Instead, she placed them inside the train.

The conductor inclined her head.

“Will she know?” Mara asked. “My mother—will she know what I chose?”

“She already did.”

The doors began to close.

Mr. Rook rushed forward. “Lysa?”

The conductor turned.

For an instant, she smiled like a seven-year-old girl.

Then the doors shut.

The black train departed Bellwether, ticking softly until the fog swallowed it. The rails shivered. A moment later, they had rusted through.

At midnight, the town waited.

No clocks struck.

Every face lifted toward the great clock above the station, but its hands had stopped one minute before twelve.

Someone screamed. Mayor Vale whispered that tomorrow had failed to come.

Then, from Mara’s shop across town, a single clock chimed.

Another answered from a house near the river.

Then another.

The station clock gave a groan, and its minute hand lurched forward.

Midnight arrived—not all at once, not perfectly, but in a wave of bells spreading through Bellwether.

Wednesday began.

It rained unexpectedly.

The baker burned his first batch of bread. Mayor Vale forgot a speech and had to speak honestly. The farmer planted winter wheat without knowing whether it would survive. At the schoolyard, the boy climbed the cedar tree.

He fell.

He landed laughing in a pile of wet leaves, then climbed again.

Years later, people still spoke of the train, though many claimed it had been a shared superstition. The tracks were removed. The station became a library. Mr. Rook retired and spent his mornings painting pictures of houses under three suns.

Mara kept her mother’s first eleven letters only in memory. Sometimes she recalled entire passages. Sometimes all she could remember was the shape of the handwriting or the feeling of paper trembling in her hands.

She married. She did not know in advance that the answer would be yes.

She had a daughter. She did not know whether the child would be healthy.

She grew older. She made mistakes no newspaper had warned her about and found joys no parcel could have contained.

On the first Tuesday of every December, Mara closed the clock shop before dawn and walked to the old platform. She stood there until sunrise, listening.

The train never returned.

Yet once, when fog covered the river and the world seemed to be holding its breath, she heard a soft ticking in the distance.

Mara waited.

The sound came closer.

For one wild moment, she wished for the black engine to emerge, for the doors to open, for one more letter to arrive with her name written in that familiar hand.

But the ticking was only rain beginning on the library roof.

Mara smiled.

She had not known it would rain.
